#### 5.3.3 New enrolments and stock {#s-d-3-3}

[]{#lab-sig-s-d-3-3}

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" title="Changed in the lab (MAC-05/06): significance stars"}
Significance stars in tables and correlation maps: \* p ≤ 0.10; \*\* p ≤ 0.05; \*\*\* p ≤ 0.01 (no correction for multiple testing). In tables, each p column gets a “(sig.)” column with the stars next to it, and rows with p ≤ 0.10 in the first p column are in **bold** (no background colour). The caption above each table says which column defines the bold rows. All tables are complete, with stars and bold in every row; tables with more than 25 rows sit in a scrollable box. In heat maps, the colour is the sign and strength of the correlation and the stars are the significance.
:::


**Method.** Correlations between annual new enrolments, year-end stock and the indicators.

**Data.** As in 5.3.1.

**How to read.** One row per pair with the coefficient.

**Interpretation.** The same caveat on sample size as in 5.3.1 applies.

*Output:* Table `tab_corr_proxies_annual`.

::: {#cell-c300 .cell execution_count=19}
``` {.python .cell-code}
rows = []
for yv in ("n_new", "stock"):
    for xv in MACRO_VARS:
        for lag in range(4):
            r, p = corr_pair(ann_m[xv].shift(lag).to_numpy().astype(float), ann_m[yv].to_numpy().astype(float), GLOBAL_METHOD)
            rows.append({"y": yv, "x": xv, "lag_years": lag, "r": r, "p_value": p, "n": int(ann_m.height - lag)})
corr_proxies = pl.DataFrame(rows)
save_tab(corr_proxies, "tab_corr_proxies_annual", fmt="{:.4g}")
corr_proxies
```

### 5.4 Panel correlations {#s-d-4}

*No new terms are introduced in this section; terms used here are defined in the Glossary.*

#### 5.4.1 Full panel {#s-d-4-1}

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" title="Changed in the lab (IMP-12): data cut at 2025"}
Paper text adjusted to the [lab window](#lab-recorte): **2016–2025**.
:::


**Method.** Correlation matrix of CDA-level variables in the full panel, with pairwise-complete observations, computed out of core in DuckDB; Spearman coefficients are Pearson correlations of average ranks.

**Data.** VAT (ICMS) CDA × year panel (1.4), legal entities only, 2016–2025; unit of observation: the CDA-year.

**How to read.** Matrix of coefficients for recovery rate, its lag, stock, age and payment indicator.

**Interpretation.** These coefficients describe the whole panel and serve as the benchmark for the estimation sample.

*Output:* Table `tab_corr_full`.

::: {#cell-c303 .cell execution_count=20}
``` {.python .cell-code}
PANEL_VARS = ["rate", "rate_l1", "stock", "age", "paid_flag"]
def panel_corr(frame: pl.DataFrame) -> pl.DataFrame:
    rows = []
    for a in PANEL_VARS:
        row = {"variable": a}
        for b in PANEL_VARS:
            row[b] = corr_pair(frame[a].to_numpy().astype(float), frame[b].to_numpy().astype(float), GLOBAL_METHOD)[0]
        rows.append(row)
    return pl.DataFrame(rows)
PANEL_SRC = parts_glob("1.4:panel", PANEL, EXTRACT_PARAMS)
PAIR_SQL = """
WITH d AS (
    SELECT CAST({a} AS DOUBLE) AS a, CAST({b} AS DOUBLE) AS b
    FROM (SELECT rate, rate_l1, LN(stock) AS stock, age, paid_flag FROM read_parquet('{src}') WHERE stock > 0)
    WHERE {a} IS NOT NULL AND {b} IS NOT NULL AND NOT isnan({a}) AND NOT isnan({b})
), r AS (
    -- average ranks for ties, as in scipy.stats.spearmanr
    SELECT a, b,
           RANK() OVER (ORDER BY a) + (COUNT(*) OVER (PARTITION BY a) - 1) / 2.0 AS ra,
           RANK() OVER (ORDER BY b) + (COUNT(*) OVER (PARTITION BY b) - 1) / 2.0 AS rb
    FROM d
)
SELECT '{a}' AS var_a, '{b}' AS var_b, COUNT(*) AS n, CORR(a, b) AS pearson, CORR(ra, rb) AS spearman FROM r
"""
PAIRS = {f"{a}__{b}": PAIR_SQL.format(a=a, b=b, src=PANEL_SRC)
         for i, a in enumerate(PANEL_VARS) for b in PANEL_VARS[i + 1:]}
pair_corr = collect(cached_sql_parts("D.4.1", PAIRS, params=EXTRACT_PARAMS))
lookup = {(r["var_a"], r["var_b"]): r[GLOBAL_METHOD] for r in pair_corr.iter_rows(named=True)}
corr_full = pl.DataFrame([{"variable": a, **{b: 1.0 if a == b else lookup.get((a, b), lookup.get((b, a))) for b in PANEL_VARS}}
                          for a in PANEL_VARS])
save_tab(corr_full, "tab_corr_full", fmt="{:.3f}")
corr_full
```

### 5.5 Statistical significance {#s-d-5}

*Terms introduced in this section:* Newey–West (HAC) standard errors; moving-block bootstrap. Definitions are given in the Glossary.

#### 5.5.1 Robust inference {#s-d-5-1}

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" title="Changed in the lab (IMP-12): data cut at 2025"}
Paper text adjusted to the [lab window](#lab-recorte): **up to December 2025**.
:::

[]{#lab-sig-s-d-5-1}

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" title="Changed in the lab (MAC-05/06): significance stars"}
Significance stars in tables and correlation maps: \* p ≤ 0.10; \*\* p ≤ 0.05; \*\*\* p ≤ 0.01 (no correction for multiple testing). In tables, each p column gets a “(sig.)” column with the stars next to it, and rows with p ≤ 0.10 in the first p column are in **bold** (no background colour). The caption above each table says which column defines the bold rows. All tables are complete, with stars and bold in every row; tables with more than 25 rows sit in a scrollable box. In heat maps, the colour is the sign and strength of the correlation and the stars are the significance.
:::


**Method.** Robust inference for correlations between autocorrelated series: the moving-block bootstrap resamples contiguous blocks of observations and so preserves short-run dependence; results are checked against Newey–West (HAC) standard errors.

**Data.** Monthly VAT (ICMS) series (1.5), January 2016 to December 2025; unit of observation: the month. Macroeconomic series from 1.6 at the same frequency.

**How to read.** One row per variable pair and lag, with the coefficient, bootstrap confidence interval and *p*-value.

**Interpretation.** Intervals that include zero indicate associations not distinguishable from zero once dependence is accounted for.

::: {#cell-c308 .cell execution_count=22}
``` {.python .cell-code}
from statsmodels.stats.sandwich_covariance import cov_hac

def block_bootstrap_corr(x: np.ndarray, y: np.ndarray, method: str, block: int = 12, n_boot: int = 999) -> tuple[float, float, float, float]:
    m = ~(np.isnan(x) | np.isnan(y))
    x, y = x[m], y[m]
    n = x.size
    r0 = corr_pair(x, y, method)[0]
    rng = np.random.default_rng(SEED)
    starts = np.arange(n - block + 1)
    boots = []
    for _ in range(n_boot):
        idx = np.concatenate([np.arange(s, s + block) for s in rng.choice(starts, size=int(np.ceil(n / block)))])[:n]
        boots.append(corr_pair(x[idx], y[idx], method)[0])
    boots = np.array(boots)
    p = float(2 * min((boots <= 0).mean(), (boots >= 0).mean()))
    return r0, float(np.percentile(boots, 2.5)), float(np.percentile(boots, 97.5)), p

def robust_monthly() -> list[dict]:
    rows = []
    for r in ccf_m.iter_rows(named=True):
        x, y = PREPARED[r["x"]], PREPARED[r["y"]]
        n = min(x.size, y.size)
        lag = r["lag_months"]
        est, lo, hi, p = block_bootstrap_corr(x[-n:][:-lag], y[-n:][lag:], METHOD.get((r["y"], r["x"]), GLOBAL_METHOD))
        rows.append({"y": r["y"], "x": r["x"], "lag": lag, "frequency": "monthly", "r": est, "ci_low": lo, "ci_high": hi, "p_boot": p})
    return rows

robust = pl.DataFrame(cached_json("D.5.1", robust_monthly, params={"block": 12, "n_boot": 999, "macro": "MAC-07: PIB e crédito reais, PNAD civil"}))
robust.sort("p_boot").head(10)
```

#### 5.5.2 Multiple testing {#s-d-5-2}

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" title="Changed in the lab (IMP-12): data cut at 2025"}
Paper text adjusted to the [lab window](#lab-recorte): **up to December 2025**.
:::


**Method.** Control of the false discovery rate across all variable–lag combinations with the Benjamini–Hochberg procedure at *q* = 0.05: among the associations declared significant, the expected share of false positives is at most 5%.

**Data.** Monthly VAT (ICMS) series (1.5), January 2016 to December 2025; unit of observation: the month. Macroeconomic series from 1.6 at the same frequency.

**How to read.** Heat map: rows are indicators, columns lags in months; colour and printed value give the correlation with monthly collection; an asterisk marks combinations significant after correction. The table lists the significant associations.

**Interpretation.** Isolated significant cells at scattered lags are weaker evidence than a consistent block across adjacent lags.

*Output:* Figure `fig_heatmap_significant`; Table `tab_assoc_significance`.

::: {#cell-c310 .cell execution_count=23}
``` {.python .cell-code}
robust = robust.with_columns(pl.Series("q_bh", multipletests(robust["p_boot"].to_numpy(), method="fdr_bh")[1]))
robust = robust.with_columns((pl.col("q_bh") < 0.05).alias("significant"))
sig = robust.filter(pl.col("y") == "collection").sort("lag")
mat = sig.pivot(on="lag", index="x", values="r", sort_columns=True)
flag = sig.pivot(on="lag", index="x", values="significant", sort_columns=True)
cols = [c for c in mat.columns if c != "x"]
marks = [[("" if v is None else f"{v:.2f}" + ("*" if f else "")) for v, f in zip(rv, fv)]
         for rv, fv in zip(mat.select(cols).iter_rows(), flag.select(cols).iter_rows())]
fig = heatmap(mat, "x", colorbar_title="Correlation with<br>collection", text=marks)
fig.add_annotation(text="* significant after Benjamini–Hochberg correction (q < 0.05)", x=0, y=-0.25, xref="paper", yref="paper",
                   showarrow=False, xanchor="left", font_size=9)
fig.update_layout(xaxis_title="Lag (months)")
save_fig(fig, "fig_heatmap_significant")
save_tab(robust.filter(pl.col("significant")).sort("q_bh"), "tab_assoc_significance", fmt="{:.4g}")
fig
```

### 5.6 CDA-level and portfolio-level models {#s-d-6}

*Terms introduced in this section:* Logit model, odds ratio, fixed effects, variance inflation factor, AR(1). Definitions are given in the Glossary.

#### 5.6.1 Model 1: probability of payment {#s-d-6-1}

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" title="Changed in the lab (IMP-12): data cut at 2025"}
Paper text adjusted to the [lab window](#lab-recorte): **2016–2025**.
:::

[]{#lab-sig-s-d-6-1}

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" title="Changed in the lab (MAC-05/06): significance stars"}
Significance stars in tables and correlation maps: \* p ≤ 0.10; \*\* p ≤ 0.05; \*\*\* p ≤ 0.01 (no correction for multiple testing). In tables, each p column gets a “(sig.)” column with the stars next to it, and rows with p ≤ 0.10 in the first p column are in **bold** (no background colour). The caption above each table says which column defines the bold rows. All tables are complete, with stars and bold in every row; tables with more than 25 rows sit in a scrollable box. In heat maps, the colour is the sign and strength of the correlation and the stars are the significance.
:::


**Method.** Logit model of the probability that a CDA records a payment in a year, as a function of log stock, age and lagged recovery rate, with year fixed effects that absorb all common shocks, including programmes and macroeconomic conditions.

**Data.** VAT (ICMS) CDA × year panel (1.4), legal entities only, 2016–2025; unit of observation: the CDA-year. Random sample of one million CDA-years with positive stock and an observed lag.

**How to read.** One row per regressor with coefficient, robust standard error, *p*-value and odds ratio.

**Interpretation.** An odds ratio above 1 means higher values of the regressor are associated with higher odds of payment, other regressors held constant.

*Output:* Table `tab_model1_logit`.

::: {#cell-c313 .cell execution_count=24}
``` {.python .cell-code}
import statsmodels.formula.api as smf
est = est_sample.with_columns(pl.col("stock").log().alias("log_stock"), pl.col("year").cast(pl.Utf8)).to_pandas()

def coef_table(res, label: str, odds: bool = False) -> pl.DataFrame:
    ci = res.conf_int()
    out = pl.DataFrame({"term": res.params.index.tolist(), "coef": res.params.values, "se": res.bse.values,
                        "p_value": res.pvalues.values, "ci_low": ci[0].values, "ci_high": ci[1].values}).with_columns(pl.lit(label).alias("model"))
    return out.with_columns(pl.col("coef").exp().alias("odds_ratio")) if odds else out

m1 = smf.logit("paid_flag ~ log_stock + age + rate_l1 + C(year)", data=est).fit(disp=False, cov_type="HC1")
tab_m1 = coef_table(m1, "logit", odds=True)
save_tab(tab_m1.filter(~pl.col("term").str.starts_with("C(year)")), "tab_model1_logit", fmt="{:.4g}")
print(f"McFadden pseudo-R2 = {m1.prsquared:.4f}; n = {int(m1.nobs):,}")
tab_m1
```

#### 5.6.2 Model 2: CDA recovery rate {#s-d-6-2}

[]{#lab-sig-s-d-6-2}

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" title="Changed in the lab (MAC-05/06): significance stars"}
Significance stars in tables and correlation maps: \* p ≤ 0.10; \*\* p ≤ 0.05; \*\*\* p ≤ 0.01 (no correction for multiple testing). In tables, each p column gets a “(sig.)” column with the stars next to it, and rows with p ≤ 0.10 in the first p column are in **bold** (no background colour). The caption above each table says which column defines the bold rows. All tables are complete, with stars and bold in every row; tables with more than 25 rows sit in a scrollable box. In heat maps, the colour is the sign and strength of the correlation and the stars are the significance.
:::


**Method.** OLS regression of the CDA recovery rate on its lag, log stock and age, with year fixed effects and heteroskedasticity-robust (HC1) standard errors; CDA-years with rates above one are excluded.

**Data.** As in 5.6.1.

**How to read.** One row per regressor with coefficient, standard error and *p*-value; R² and sample size are printed.

**Interpretation.** The coefficient on the lagged rate measures persistence of recovery at the CDA level.

*Output:* Table `tab_model2_ols`.

::: {#cell-c315 .cell execution_count=25}
``` {.python .cell-code}
m2 = smf.ols("rate ~ rate_l1 + log_stock + age + C(year)", data=est[est["rate"] <= 1]).fit(cov_type="HC1")
tab_m2 = coef_table(m2, "ols")
save_tab(tab_m2.filter(~pl.col("term").str.starts_with("C(year)")), "tab_model2_ols", fmt="{:.4g}")
print(f"R2 = {m2.rsquared:.4f}; n = {int(m2.nobs):,}")
tab_m2
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}
```
R2 = 0.0250; n = 993,579
```
:::

#### 5.6.3 Model 3: portfolio recovery rate {#s-d-6-3}

[]{#lab-sig-s-d-6-3}

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" title="Changed in the lab (MAC-05/06): significance stars"}
Significance stars in tables and correlation maps: \* p ≤ 0.10; \*\* p ≤ 0.05; \*\*\* p ≤ 0.01 (no correction for multiple testing). In tables, each p column gets a “(sig.)” column with the stars next to it, and rows with p ≤ 0.10 in the first p column are in **bold** (no background colour). The caption above each table says which column defines the bold rows. All tables are complete, with stars and bold in every row; tables with more than 25 rows sit in a scrollable box. In heat maps, the colour is the sign and strength of the correlation and the stars are the significance.
:::


**Method.** First-order autoregression of the portfolio recovery rate, r_t = α + ρ r_{t−1} + ε_t, at annual and monthly frequency, with Newey–West standard errors (12 lags) at monthly frequency; only finite rates enter the estimation.

**Data.** Annual rates (3.1.1) and monthly rates (4.4.2).

**How to read.** One row per frequency and term, with coefficient, standard error, *p*-value and number of observations.

**Interpretation.** ρ near 0 indicates that shocks to recovery do not carry over; ρ near 1 indicates highly persistent recovery.

*Output:* Table `tab_model3_ar1`.

::: {#cell-c317 .cell execution_count=26}
``` {.python .cell-code}
from statsmodels.tsa.ar_model import AutoReg
y_a = annual["portfolio_rate"].drop_nulls().to_numpy()
y_m = monthly_rate["rate"].drop_nulls().to_numpy()
ar_a = AutoReg(y_a[np.isfinite(y_a)], lags=1).fit()
ar_m = AutoReg(y_m[np.isfinite(y_m)], lags=1).fit(cov_type="HAC", cov_kwds={"maxlags": 12})
tab_m3 = pl.DataFrame([{"frequency": f, "term": t, "coef": float(r.params[i]), "se": float(r.bse[i]), "p_value": float(r.pvalues[i]), "n": int(r.nobs)}
                       for f, r in (("annual", ar_a), ("monthly", ar_m)) for i, t in enumerate(("const", "rate_lag1"))])
save_tab(tab_m3, "tab_model3_ar1", fmt="{:.4g}")
tab_m3
```

#### 5.6.4 Model 4: probability of payment and macroeconomic conditions {#s-d-6-4}

[]{#lab-sig-s-d-6-4}

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" title="Changed in the lab (MAC-05/06): significance stars"}
Significance stars in tables and correlation maps: \* p ≤ 0.10; \*\* p ≤ 0.05; \*\*\* p ≤ 0.01 (no correction for multiple testing). In tables, each p column gets a “(sig.)” column with the stars next to it, and rows with p ≤ 0.10 in the first p column are in **bold** (no background colour). The caption above each table says which column defines the bold rows. All tables are complete, with stars and bold in every row; tables with more than 25 rows sit in a scrollable box. In heat maps, the colour is the sign and strength of the correlation and the stars are the significance.
:::


**Method.** Model 1 with year fixed effects replaced by five annual macroeconomic indicators (Selic, IPCA, IBC-Br, credit to firms, unemployment), each standardised to zero mean and unit variance; collinearity is assessed with variance inflation factors.

**Data.** As in 5.6.1, merged with annual macroeconomic series.

**How to read.** Coefficient table as in 5.6.1, plus a table of VIFs.

**Interpretation.** Odds ratios refer to a one-standard-deviation change in the indicator. VIFs above about 10 mean that individual coefficients are poorly identified.

*Output:* Tables `tab_model4_logit_macro`, `tab_vif`.

::: {#cell-c319 .cell execution_count=27}
``` {.python .cell-code}
from statsmodels.stats.outliers_influence import variance_inflation_factor
macro_std = macro_a.with_columns([((pl.col(c) - pl.col(c).mean()) / pl.col(c).std()).alias(c) for c in MACRO_VARS])
est_m = est_sample.with_columns(pl.col("stock").log().alias("log_stock")).join(macro_std, on="year", how="left").drop_nulls(MACRO_VARS).to_pandas()
MAIN_MACRO = ["selic", "ipca", "gdp_monthly", "credit_firms", "unemployment"]
m4 = smf.logit("paid_flag ~ log_stock + age + rate_l1 + " + " + ".join(MAIN_MACRO), data=est_m).fit(disp=False, cov_type="HC1")
tab_m4 = coef_table(m4, "logit_macro", odds=True)
Xv = macro_std.select(MAIN_MACRO).drop_nulls().to_numpy()
vif = pl.DataFrame({"variable": MAIN_MACRO, "vif": [variance_inflation_factor(np.column_stack([np.ones(len(Xv)), Xv]), i + 1) for i in range(len(MAIN_MACRO))]})
save_tab(tab_m4, "tab_model4_logit_macro", fmt="{:.4g}")
save_tab(vif, "tab_vif", fmt="{:.2f}")
tab_m4
```

#### 5.6.5 Model 4b: principal components {#s-d-6-5}

[]{#lab-sig-s-d-6-5}

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" title="Changed in the lab (MAC-05/06): significance stars"}
Significance stars in tables and correlation maps: \* p ≤ 0.10; \*\* p ≤ 0.05; \*\*\* p ≤ 0.01 (no correction for multiple testing). In tables, each p column gets a “(sig.)” column with the stars next to it, and rows with p ≤ 0.10 in the first p column are in **bold** (no background colour). The caption above each table says which column defines the bold rows. All tables are complete, with stars and bold in every row; tables with more than 25 rows sit in a scrollable box. In heat maps, the colour is the sign and strength of the correlation and the stars are the significance.
:::


**Method.** Model 4 estimated on the principal components of the standardised indicators, which are uncorrelated by construction.

**Data.** As in 5.6.4.

**How to read.** Loadings table: weight of each indicator in each component; coefficient table as in 5.6.1.

**Interpretation.** Interpret a component's coefficient through its loadings, for example as a general activity or price factor.

*Output:* Tables `tab_pca_loadings`, `tab_model4b_pcs`.

::: {#cell-c321 .cell execution_count=28}
``` {.python .cell-code}
from sklearn.decomposition import PCA as _PCA
Z = macro_std.drop_nulls(MACRO_VARS)
pca_macro = _PCA(n_components=3, random_state=SEED).fit(Z.select(MACRO_VARS).to_numpy())
loadings = pl.DataFrame({"variable": MACRO_VARS, **{f"PC{i + 1}": pca_macro.components_[i] for i in range(3)}})
pcs = pl.DataFrame({"year": Z["year"], **{f"PC{i + 1}": pca_macro.transform(Z.select(MACRO_VARS).to_numpy())[:, i] for i in range(3)}})
est_pc = est_sample.with_columns(pl.col("stock").log().alias("log_stock")).join(pcs, on="year", how="inner").to_pandas()
m4b = smf.logit("paid_flag ~ log_stock + age + rate_l1 + PC1 + PC2 + PC3", data=est_pc).fit(disp=False, cov_type="HC1")
tab_m4b = coef_table(m4b, "logit_pcs", odds=True)
save_tab(loadings.with_columns(pl.lit(None).alias("_")).drop("_"), "tab_pca_loadings", fmt="{:.3f}")
save_tab(tab_m4b, "tab_model4b_pcs", fmt="{:.4g}")
print("Explained variance:", np.round(pca_macro.explained_variance_ratio_, 3))
tab_m4b
```

#### 5.6.6 Model comparison {#s-d-6-6}

[]{#lab-sig-s-d-6-6}

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" title="Changed in the lab (MAC-05/06): significance stars"}
Significance stars in tables and correlation maps: \* p ≤ 0.10; \*\* p ≤ 0.05; \*\*\* p ≤ 0.01 (no correction for multiple testing). In tables, each p column gets a “(sig.)” column with the stars next to it, and rows with p ≤ 0.10 in the first p column are in **bold** (no background colour). The caption above each table says which column defines the bold rows. All tables are complete, with stars and bold in every row; tables with more than 25 rows sit in a scrollable box. In heat maps, the colour is the sign and strength of the correlation and the stars are the significance.
:::


**Method.** Comparison of specifications by McFadden's pseudo-R² and likelihood-ratio tests between nested models.

**Data.** Models of 5.6.1, 5.6.4 and 5.6.5.

**How to read.** One row per model or comparison.

**Interpretation.** The fixed-effects model is the upper benchmark for specifications based on annual common variables, because year dummies absorb all of their variation.

*Output:* Table `tab_model_comparison`.

::: {#cell-c323 .cell execution_count=29}
``` {.python .cell-code}
base = smf.logit("paid_flag ~ log_stock + age + rate_l1", data=est_m).fit(disp=False)
fe = smf.logit("paid_flag ~ log_stock + age + rate_l1 + C(year)", data=est_m.assign(year=est_m["year"].astype(str))).fit(disp=False)
macro_fit = smf.logit("paid_flag ~ log_stock + age + rate_l1 + " + " + ".join(MAIN_MACRO), data=est_m).fit(disp=False)
pc_fit = smf.logit("paid_flag ~ log_stock + age + rate_l1 + PC1 + PC2 + PC3", data=est_pc).fit(disp=False)
def lr(a, b) -> tuple[float, float]:
    stat = 2 * (b.llf - a.llf)
    return float(stat), float(stats.chi2.sf(stat, b.df_model - a.df_model))
comparison = pl.DataFrame([{"model": n, "pseudo_r2": float(r.prsquared), "aic": float(r.aic), "df_model": int(r.df_model),
                            "lr_vs_base": lr(base, r)[0] if n != "CDA variables only" else float("nan"),
                            "p_lr": lr(base, r)[1] if n != "CDA variables only" else float("nan")}
                           for n, r in (("CDA variables only", base), ("Year fixed effects", fe), ("Macro indicators", macro_fit), ("Macro PCs", pc_fit))])
save_tab(comparison, "tab_model_comparison", fmt="{:.4g}")
comparison
```

### 5.7 Dynamic models {#s-d-7}

*Terms introduced in this section:* ARDL, Granger causality. Definitions are given in the Glossary.

#### 5.7.1 Autoregressive distributed-lag models {#s-d-7-1}

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" title="Changed in the lab (IMP-12): data cut at 2025"}
Paper text adjusted to the [lab window](#lab-recorte): **up to December 2025**.
:::

[]{#lab-sig-s-d-7-1}

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" title="Changed in the lab (MAC-05/06): significance stars"}
Significance stars in tables and correlation maps: \* p ≤ 0.10; \*\* p ≤ 0.05; \*\*\* p ≤ 0.01 (no correction for multiple testing). In tables, each p column gets a “(sig.)” column with the stars next to it, and rows with p ≤ 0.10 in the first p column are in **bold** (no background colour). The caption above each table says which column defines the bold rows. All tables are complete, with stars and bold in every row; tables with more than 25 rows sit in a scrollable box. In heat maps, the colour is the sign and strength of the correlation and the stars are the significance.
:::


**Method.** Autoregressive distributed-lag (ARDL) models of each stationary monthly portfolio series on its own lags and on current and lagged indicators, with programme dummies; lag orders selected by an information criterion; Newey–West standard errors.

**Data.** Monthly VAT (ICMS) series (1.5), January 2016 to December 2025; unit of observation: the month. Macroeconomic series from 1.6 at the same frequency. Pooled portfolio and by origin.

**How to read.** One row per model and regressor with coefficient, standard error and *p*-value.

**Interpretation.** Significant lagged indicators suggest delayed associations; coefficients are conditional on the programme dummies.

*Output:* Table `tab_ardl`.

::: {#cell-c326 .cell execution_count=30}
``` {.python .cell-code}
from statsmodels.tsa.ardl import ardl_select_order
PROG_DUMMY = np.zeros(prepared_df.height)
months = prepared_df["month"].to_numpy()
for _, a, b in PROGRAMMES:
    PROG_DUMMY[(months >= np.datetime64(a)) & (months <= np.datetime64(b))] = 1
rows = []
for yv in ("collection", "n_payers"):
    if yv not in prepared_df.columns:
        continue
    X = prepared_df.select([c for c in MAIN_MACRO if c in prepared_df.columns]).to_pandas()
    sel = ardl_select_order(prepared_df[yv].to_numpy(), maxlag=3, exog=X, maxorder=6, ic="aic", trend="c",
                            fixed=PROG_DUMMY[:, None], seasonal=True, period=12)
    res = sel.model.fit(cov_type="HAC", cov_kwds={"maxlags": 12})
    rows += [{"y": yv, "term": t, "coef": float(c), "se": float(s), "p_value": float(p)}
             for t, c, s, p in zip(res.params.index, res.params.values, res.bse.values, res.pvalues.values)]
ardl = pl.DataFrame(rows)
save_tab(ardl.filter(~pl.col("term").str.contains("s\\(")), "tab_ardl", fmt="{:.4g}")
ardl
```

#### 5.7.2 Granger causality {#s-d-7-2}

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" title="Changed in the lab (IMP-12): data cut at 2025"}
Paper text adjusted to the [lab window](#lab-recorte): **up to December 2025**.
:::

[]{#lab-sig-s-d-7-2}

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" title="Changed in the lab (MAC-05/06): significance stars"}
Significance stars in tables and correlation maps: \* p ≤ 0.10; \*\* p ≤ 0.05; \*\*\* p ≤ 0.01 (no correction for multiple testing). In tables, each p column gets a “(sig.)” column with the stars next to it, and rows with p ≤ 0.10 in the first p column are in **bold** (no background colour). The caption above each table says which column defines the bold rows. All tables are complete, with stars and bold in every row; tables with more than 25 rows sit in a scrollable box. In heat maps, the colour is the sign and strength of the correlation and the stars are the significance.
:::


**Method.** Granger tests: an indicator Granger-causes a portfolio series if its past values improve the prediction of the series beyond the series' own past. The test is an *F* test of the lagged indicator in a vector autoregression with lag length selected by AIC; *q*-values apply the Benjamini–Hochberg correction.

**Data.** Monthly VAT (ICMS) series (1.5), January 2016 to December 2025; unit of observation: the month. Macroeconomic series from 1.6 at the same frequency.

**How to read.** One row per pair with selected lags, *F* statistic, *p*-value and *q*-value.

**Interpretation.** A significant result means predictive precedence, not causation.

*Output:* Table `tab_granger`.

::: {#cell-c328 .cell execution_count=31}
``` {.python .cell-code}
from statsmodels.tsa.stattools import grangercausalitytests
from statsmodels.tsa.api import VAR
rows = []
for yv in ("collection", "n_payers"):
    for xv in MAIN_MACRO:
        d = prepared_df.select(yv, xv).drop_nulls().to_numpy()
        p_sel = max(1, VAR(d).select_order(maxlags=12).aic)
        res = grangercausalitytests(d, maxlag=[p_sel])[p_sel][0]["ssr_ftest"]
        rows.append({"y": yv, "x": xv, "lags": int(p_sel), "F": float(res[0]), "p_value": float(res[1])})
granger = pl.DataFrame(rows).with_columns(pl.Series("q_bh", multipletests([r["p_value"] for r in rows], method="fdr_bh")[1]))
save_tab(granger, "tab_granger", fmt="{:.4g}")
granger
```

#### 5.7.3 The Selic rate and tax non-payment as financing {#s-d-7-3}

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" title="Changed in the lab (IMP-12): data cut at 2025"}
Paper text adjusted to the [lab window](#lab-recorte): **up to December 2025**.
:::

[]{#lab-sig-s-d-7-3}

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" title="Changed in the lab (MAC-05/06): significance stars"}
Significance stars in tables and correlation maps: \* p ≤ 0.10; \*\* p ≤ 0.05; \*\*\* p ≤ 0.01 (no correction for multiple testing). In tables, each p column gets a “(sig.)” column with the stars next to it, and rows with p ≤ 0.10 in the first p column are in **bold** (no background colour). The caption above each table says which column defines the bold rows. All tables are complete, with stars and bold in every row; tables with more than 25 rows sit in a scrollable box. In heat maps, the colour is the sign and strength of the correlation and the stars are the significance.
:::


**Method.** Interpretation of the Selic coefficients for stock and recovery under the hypothesis that firms use unpaid taxes as financing when credit is expensive (H4b), with and without credit to firms as a control.

**Data.** Monthly VAT (ICMS) series (1.5), January 2016 to December 2025; unit of observation: the month. Macroeconomic series from 1.6 at the same frequency.

**How to read.** One row per outcome and specification with the Selic coefficient and its robust standard error.

**Interpretation.** Under H4b, a higher Selic would be associated with a larger stock and lower recovery; robustness to the credit control indicates that the association is not merely a credit-cycle effect.

*Output:* Table `tab_selic`.

::: {#cell-c330 .cell execution_count=32}
``` {.python .cell-code}
selic_rows = []
for yv in ("collection", "stock", "n_payers"):
    if yv not in prepared_df.columns:
        continue
    for spec, extra in (("Selic", []), ("Selic + credit to firms", ["credit_firms"])):
        d = prepared_df.select(yv, "selic", *extra).drop_nulls().to_pandas()
        for lag in (0, 3, 6, 12):
            dd = d.assign(selic_l=d["selic"].shift(lag)).dropna()
            res = smf.ols(f"{yv} ~ selic_l" + "".join(f" + {e}" for e in extra), data=dd).fit(cov_type="HAC", cov_kwds={"maxlags": 12})
            selic_rows.append({"y": yv, "specification": spec, "lag_months": lag, "coef_selic": float(res.params["selic_l"]),
                               "se": float(res.bse["selic_l"]), "p_value": float(res.pvalues["selic_l"]), "n": int(res.nobs)})
selic_tab = pl.DataFrame(selic_rows)
save_tab(selic_tab, "tab_selic", fmt="{:.4g}")
selic_tab
```

### 5.8 Overnight Selic rate and check of the macroeconomic correlations {#lab-macro}

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple" title="New in the lab (MAC-03, MAC-07): Macro × debt: overnight Selic instead of the target rate and check of the correlation data"}
Do the correlations with the Selic rate change when the effective (overnight) rate is used instead of the target? Are the macro data in the correlations right in source, unit, frequency, lag and coverage? Where does the correlation between employment and stock come from? Full content of the lab entry `lab/eda/2026-10-23_macro_selic_over_checagem.qmd`, assembled from its _freeze (nothing is executed here).
:::

**Data:** `macro.duckdb` (table `MACRO`, SGS/BCB series), the SGS 4189 series downloaded from the BCB on 23/10/2026 and the aggregates of the full EDA (monthly series of collections, payers and new CDAs; annual stock of the VAT (ICMS) panel). `extracao=2026-03`.
**Window:** 2016 to 2025.
**Status:** exploration and data check. Correlation is not effect.



#### 5.8.1 Overnight Selic instead of the target Selic (MAC-03) {#mac-overnight-selic-instead-of-the-target-selic-mac-03}

**Sources checked in the BCB open data catalogue on 23/10/2026:**

- **SGS 432**, used until now: *Interest rate, Selic target set by Copom*, in % p.a. It is the target, which changes only at Copom meetings.
- **SGS 4189**: *Interest rate, Selic compounded over the month, annualised on a 252-day basis*, in % p.a., monthly. According to the BCB, it is the "adjusted average rate of one-business-day repurchase operations backed by federal government securities held in custody at Selic", that is, the effective (overnight) Selic, already in the same unit as the target.
- **Discarded:** SGS 1178 (Selic annualised on a 252-day basis) is the same rate at daily frequency. The monthly version 4189 avoids an extra aggregation.

::: {#tbl-mac-selic .cell tbl-cap='Target Selic (monthly mean of the daily series 432) and overnight Selic (4189), 2016 to 2025.' execution_count=2}

Target Selic (monthly mean) and overnight Selic (4189), % p.a., 2016–2025.
:::
:::


**How to read:** the overnight rate is always slightly below the target (about 0.1 p.p.) and changes within the month, instead of changing only on Copom dates. In the tables below, the correlations with the overnight rate and with the target coincide to the third decimal place. The switch is a matter of definitional rigour and changes no result.

**What not to conclude:** with 10 years, the confidence intervals are very wide. The monthly series have strong autocorrelation, and the correlation in levels mixes common trends. There are 24 monthly and 8 annual pairs in the two tables, with no correction for multiple comparisons.

The tables in this subsection use only the first convention.

##### 5.8.2.5 The employment × stock anomaly {#mac-the-employment-stock-anomaly}

**How to read:**

- **Levels:** for 2016 to 2025 the correlation stays high. Without 2020 it is a little lower.
- **Differences:** in first differences, Pearson stays high, but Spearman is close to zero and negative. The gap between the two shows that the correlation of the changes depends on a few points. Without the changes involving 2020, the correlation changes sign and the interval includes zero. All of the correlation of the changes comes from 2020: employment fell and the summed stock of the panel also fell, and both rose again afterwards.
- **Trend and 2020:** removing only the linear trend does not eliminate the correlation, and without 2020 the interval includes zero. The pattern "rises, falls in 2020, rises again" is the same in both series.
- **The 2020 fall seems to come from the extraction:** the stock falls from BRL 410.6 bn (2019) to BRL 328.9 bn (2020), and the number of CDAs in the panel falls with it (from 2.18 mn to 1.81 mn). Such a large and simultaneous fall in the CDA count suggests that it comes from how the 2020 data were extracted (CDAs that leave and return to the panel, or extraction coverage), not from the economy. This should be checked when the corrected DEBITO table arrives.

**What not to conclude:** with 9 or 10 points, none of these correlations supports a claim in the article.

#### 5.8.3 Corrected correlations (MAC-07, 26/10/2026) {#mac-corrected-correlations-mac-07-26102026}

What could be corrected, based on the check above:

| Problem (subsection) | Correction applied |
|---|---|
| Two lag conventions (2.2) | A single one: **Y in month t against the macro in t − k**, k = 0 to 3 (the macro leads). The `Y_lk` rows of the full EDA (lagged Y) are dropped. |
| Correlation window (2.3) | Only **2016-01 to 2025-12** (120 months; 10 years). |
| Nominal GDP and corporate credit (2.2) | **Deflated by the IPCA** (SGS 433): chained index of the monthly changes, base Dec 2025 = 1. They are in BRL of Dec 2025. |
| PNAD Contínua (2.2) | Confirmed in the IBGE and SGS metadata: the monthly value of unemployment (24369) and employed persons (24379) is the **moving quarter** ending in the month, and neighbouring months share two months of interviews. In the annual series, the mean of the four calendar quarters (Mar, Jun, Sep, Dec) is used. In the monthly series, the value stays as it is, with this caveat: the monthly change is that of a moving quarter, not of a month. |
| Selic | Overnight (4189) instead of the target (MAC-03). |
| 2020 fall in the stock (2.5) | **Cannot be corrected now:** depends on the corrected DEBITO table (EQ-02/EQ-05). See the warning below. |

::: {.callout-warning title="Warning: employment × stock and the year 2020"}
The annual correlation between stock and employed persons rests on the common trend and on the 2020 fall. In that year the panel's stock falls
from BRL 410.6 bn to BRL 328.9 bn and the CDA count falls with it, which looks like an effect of the DEBITO extraction, not of the economy.
Until the corrected DEBITO arrives (EQ-02/EQ-05), no annual correlation with the stock should go into the article's text.
:::

**How to read:** "before" is the number saved by the full EDA, "after" is the same pair with the corrections. In the monthly series, the largest
change is that of deflated corporate credit (see the summary by series). In the other series, the change comes from the 2025 cut-off and,
in the rows with k ≥ 1, from the switch of lag convention. In the annual series, with 10 points, the confidence intervals are wide
(CI columns), and several correlations change considerably with the switch to real values and calendar quarters.

**What not to conclude:** the corrections remove construction biases, but do not solve the sample size (10 years), the
autocorrelation of the monthly series or the 2020 fall in the stock. The employment × stock correlation stays out of the text
until the corrected DEBITO.

#### 5.8.4 Summary of the check {#mac-summary-of-the-check}

- **Source and unit:** the 11 series come from the SGS/BCB, with name and unit recorded in the table. Target (432) and overnight (4189) are in the same unit (% p.a.).
- **Coverage:** this subsection computes the correlations for 2016 to 2025.
- **Nominal × real:** monthly GDP and corporate credit enter in current BRL, with no deflator or log. In levels, the correlation with the nominal stock captures the common trend.
- **Frequency:** daily series (target, PTAX) become monthly means. The monthly PNAD Contínua is a moving quarter (checked on 26/10/2026); subsection 3 uses calendar quarters in the annual series.
- **Lags:** there are two conventions in the EDA (lagged macro and lagged Y). Subsection 3 uses only the lagged macro.
- **Employment × stock:** the correlation replicates (0.873) and rests on the common trend and the 2020 trough, which also appears in the CDA count. Before interpreting, check the 2020 stock in the corrected DEBITO. See 2.5.

<!-- parte: 08_parte_e -->

## 6. Discussion {#s-part-e}

*No new terms are introduced in this section; terms used here are defined in the Glossary.*

### 6.1 Synthesis {#s-e-1}

The answers to the research questions are summarised in the manuscript on the basis of the results above.

### 6.2 Limitations {#s-e-2}

The analysis relies on a single frozen extraction; stocks are reconstructed from monthly snapshots; settlement is only approximated; the annual sample is short; settlement programmes introduce structural breaks; firm-level revenue and indebtedness are not available; and the restriction to VAT (ICMS) limits generalisation to other taxes.

### 6.3 Ethical considerations {#s-e-3}

The study uses only data on legal entities. Records whose debtor is identified by a CPF (natural persons) are excluded at extraction, and no name or personal identifier is retained.

### 6.4 Future research {#s-e-4}

Directions for further work include the recovered-over-recoverable indicator under a validated criterion; explicit modelling of settlement programmes through their attributes, with separate components for regular and programme-driven collection; instalment agreements and their breach; protest; the distinction between inability to pay and concealment of assets; firm indebtedness; and heterogeneity across sectors.

## 7. Correspondence with the manuscript and the dissertation {#s-7}
The structure of this notebook corresponds to the paper and to the master's dissertation prepared with the School of Technology (FT-Unicamp) thesis template.

| Notebook | Paper | Dissertation |
|---|---|---|
| Research questions | Introduction | Ch. 1 Introduction |
| 0–1 | Data | Ch. 3 Data and methods |
| Section 2 | The portfolio across tax types | Ch. 4 Exploratory analysis |
| Section 3 | The VAT (ICMS) portfolio (incl. the most concentrated CDAs) | Ch. 4 Exploratory analysis |
| Section 4 | Statistical properties (Methods) | Ch. 3 Data and methods |
| Section 5 | Macroeconomic conditions | Ch. 5 Macroeconomic associations |
| Section 6 | Discussion, limitations, conclusion | Ch. 6 Discussion; Ch. 7 Conclusion |
| 2.1.2, 2.3.1, 1.7 | Appendix | Appendices |

Figures (`fig_*.pdf`) and tables (`tab_*.tex`) are shared by the paper and the dissertation.

#### 8.2.1 How to read {#edac-how-to-read}

Each row = one **table** of the PGE/CEMEPI database. **Rows** = how many records exist. **Largest % nulls** = the fields that are missing most (e.g. fees, or CPF when there is only a CNPJ). Date range = from the oldest to the most recent in that field.

#### 8.2.2 Next (presentation) {#edac-next-presentation}

Lean suggestion for the supervisor: 1 slide "what is in the database" (volume bars) + 1 "where data are missing" (nulls) + a glossary of the 3–4 tables we will use in the model (DEBITO, ARRECADACAO, macro series). Step 2 (VAT (ICMS)/IPVA/fees mapping) feeds the next visual block.

### 8.3 Debt type in four groups: VAT (ICMS), IPVA, ITCMD and fees (TAXAS) (stock at the cut-off) {#edac-debt-type-in-four-groups-vat-icms-ipva-itcmd-and-fees-taxas-stock-at-the-cut-off}

**Stakeholder metric — value by group:** stock of `VALOR_SEM_HONORARIOS` **in a single extraction cut-off** (`ANO_EXTRACAO` × `MES_EXTRACAO`), with **1 row per `ID_DEBITO`** (CDA).

#### 8.3.1 Pitfall: summing all extractions {#edac-pitfall-summing-all-extractions}

Each CDA reappears in every extraction month. `SUM(VALOR_SEM_HONORARIOS)` over the whole table **multiplies the stock by the number of months** the debt stayed in `DEBITO`. The real VAT (ICMS) stock is in the **hundreds of billions** (the VAT (ICMS) panel is in the hundreds of BRL bn), not trillions.

#### 8.3.2 What this step does {#edac-what-this-step-does}

1. Picks the **last valid YEAR×MONTH** (month 1–12, plausible year; skips a partial load if the last month has < 80% of the median of the previous 6). Override: `CORTE = (ano, mes)` at the top of the cell.
2. Filters only that cut-off → `GROUP BY ID_DEBITO` (defensive dedup) → aggregates by `TIPO_DEBITO` → groups.
3. Writes `tipo_debito_buckets.csv` (by raw type), `tipo_debito_buckets_resumo.csv` (by group), `idade_cda_por_bucket.csv` (includes the **Base geral** (overall base) row) and regenerates the composition and age figures.

**Classification rule (order):**
1. name contains `IPVA` → **IPVA**;
2. contains `ICMS` → **VAT (ICMS)** (VAT);
3. contains `ITCMD`, or `ITBI` with `Doação`/`Causa Mortis` (old name of the inheritance and gift tax) → **ITCMD**;
4. the rest (fines, court fees, reimbursements, contributions etc.) → **TAXAS** (fees).

The `regra` (rule) column stays in the CSV. **Self-contained** cell (needs only step 0): run only this code cell, never Restart+Run All.

#### 8.3.3 How to read (after the cut-off) {#edac-how-to-read-after-the-cut-off}

`n_id` = distinct CDAs **at the cut-off**. `soma_valor` = `VALOR_SEM_HONORARIOS` stock **of that month** (once per CDA): compare with collections / panel; it is **not** a sum over months.

Expected order of magnitude for VAT (ICMS): **hundreds of billions**, not trillions. If the chart goes above ~BRL 2 tn, the cut-off filter failed.

`n_linhas` in the CSV can still be > `n_id` if the same ID appears more than once *within* the month; the stock used is `MAX(valor)` per ID.

If an important label falls into TAXAS by mistake, adjust `bucket_de` / `bucket_sql` and re-run **only the code cell** above.

::: {#edac-8c1112fe .cell execution_count=18}

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

OK $EDA_ARTIFACTS/_pdf_figs/fig_bucket_valor.png
If MISS: re-run the step 2 code cell (snapshot).

### 8.4 Descriptives — VAT (ICMS) | IPVA | ITCMD | fees (TAXAS) {#edac-descriptives-vat-icms-ipva-itcmd-fees-taxas}

Uses the step 2 CSV (`tipo_debito_buckets.csv`) **already at the cut-off level** (1 CDA). Contrast: **IPVA by count** vs **VAT (ICMS) by value**; ITCMD is small in count but with a high mean value per CDA.

CDA age: `idade_anos = (end of the cut-off month − DATA_INSCRICAO)/365.25`, mean and median by group and for the **overall base** (all CDAs at the cut-off), also generated in the snapshot cell (without scanning all extractions).

#### 8.4.1 How to read % count vs % value {#edac-how-to-read-count-vs-value}

If IPVA has a high `pct_qtd` and a low `pct_valor`, there are many debts of low unit value. VAT (ICMS) with the opposite justifies focusing the panel/models on VAT (ICMS). ITCMD appears as a group of its own: few CDAs, high mean value.

The percentages use the **stock at the cut-off** (not the sum of all extractions).

::: {#edac-f5bc94d2 .cell execution_count=21}

### 8.6 Correlations and memory of the rate (VAT (ICMS) panel) {#edac-correlations-and-memory-of-the-rate-vat-icms-panel}

From the step 4 parquet: CDA age, rate in the **previous year** and **two / three years before** (within each `ID_DEBITO`), linear and monotone (Spearman) correlation, and a heatmap.

Memory: DuckDB on the parquet (without loading 23M rows into Python), temp on Meedi, `threads=2` / `3GB`.

#### 8.6.1 What linear correlation, Spearman and "years before" are (as used here) {#edac-what-linear-correlation-spearman-and-years-before-are-as-used-here}

**Linear correlation (Pearson)** measures *linear* association between two continuous variables (values from −1 to +1). Here: linear relationship between `taxa`, stock, age and the rate itself in previous years.

**Spearman** is the linear correlation of the *ranks*: it captures monotone (not only linear) association. Useful if rate outliers distort the linear correlation.

**Rate k years before** in the panel: the value of the same CDA *k* years earlier. Partitioning by `ID_DEBITO` and ordering by `ano` (year), we look at the rate of the same debt 1, 2 or 3 years before.

This tests the persistence of collections relative to the stock (does last year's recovery rate help predict today's?).

Classic references: Spearman (1904); definition of autocorrelation in panels in Wooldridge, *Econometric Analysis of Cross Section and Panel Data*.

#### 8.6.2 How to read the heatmap {#edac-how-to-read-the-heatmap}

Cells close to **+1**: the two series rise/fall together (Pearson linear; Spearman monotone). Close to **0**: little linear/monotone association. High values in `taxa × taxa_l1` (and `l2`/`l3`) indicate **persistence** of the collection rate on the same debt, a useful signal for the step 6 models.

`idade_anos × taxa`: if negative, older CDAs tend to collect less relative to the stock (descriptive reading, not causal).

### 8.7 Three models on the VAT (ICMS) panel (annual level) {#edac-three-models-on-the-vat-icms-panel-annual-level}

Based on section 5 (persistence in the **previous year's** rate), we fit three simple readings, **still descriptive**, not causal, on the `ID_DEBITO × year` panel:

1. **Logit**: probability of collecting anything in the year (`arrecadado > 0`).
2. **Rate regression**: how much is collected relative to the stock.
3. **Aggregate series**: stock, collections and the portfolio recovery rate in the year (PGE's "cash" view), **each in its own chart** (no dual axis).

The current panel is **annual** (there is no quarter in step 4). If a quarterly calendar is needed, we cut one later from `ARRECADACAO` with month.

Micro fit: random sample of **1 million** rows with the previous year's rate filled in (fixed seed), to fit in the Mac's RAM. The aggregate series uses **all** years of the parquet.

#### 8.7.1 What each model estimates (definition) {#edac-what-each-model-estimates-definition}

**Logit.** Indicator Y = 1 if the debt collected in the year and 0 otherwise. The model estimates the probability of payment as a function of the covariates (logistic curve).

Covariates: lagged rate (`taxa_l1`), log(1 + stock), CDA age in years, and year dummies.

**Rate (OLS).** Linear regression of `taxa` on the same covariates (without the contemporaneous rate on the right-hand side).

**Aggregate.** In each year: sum of the stock, sum of collections and portfolio rate = total collections / total stock. Shows the trajectory of the VAT (ICMS) portfolio as a whole.

Interpretation for state attorneys: coefficients express **association** (controlling for year and stock), not policy effect.

#### 8.7.2 How to read the coefficients (logit and rate) {#edac-how-to-read-the-coefficients-logit-and-rate}

In the **logit**, a positive coefficient on `taxa_l1` means: debts that collected more in the previous year have a **higher chance** of collecting again (all else constant in the sample). The value itself is not a direct "% more": also look at the average marginal effect printed below.

In the **rate regression**, a `taxa_l1` coefficient close to 0.5 echoes the section 5 correlation: about half of the past rate "reappears" in the current rate, on a linear average.

`ano` (year) dummies absorb common shocks (fiscal calendar, COVID, etc.).

#### 8.7.3 Model 1M — Logit with CDA variables and annual macroeconomics {#edac-model-1m-logit-with-cda-variables-and-annual-macroeconomics}

**Question.** After controlling for previous recovery, stock and CDA age, is the year's macroeconomic environment associated with the chance that the VAT (ICMS) CDA has some payment (GARE) in that year?

**Dependent variable.** $y_{it}=1$ if CDA $i$ had collections $>0$ in year $t$; $0$ otherwise.

**Logit model** (McFadden, 1974):
$$\Pr(y_{it}=1)=\Lambda\big(\beta_0+\beta_1\,\text{rate}_{i,t-1}+\beta_2\ln(1+\text{stock}_{it})+\beta_3\,\text{age}_{it}+\gamma'\,\mathbf{m}_t\big),\qquad \Lambda(u)=\frac{1}{1+e^{-u}}$$
where $\mathbf{m}_t$ are annual means of the macro series (BCB SGS), standardised over the period ($z=(x-\bar x)/s$): each $\gamma$ is the change in log-odds for +1 standard deviation of the macro variable. Fit: McFadden's pseudo-$R^2$ $=1-\ln L_{\text{model}}/\ln L_{\text{intercept only}}$.

**Why the year dummies drop out when the macro series enter.** An annual macro variable is the same for all CDAs in the same year, so it is an exact linear combination of the year dummies (the code checks the rank of the matrix at the annual grain). With 9 years (2017–2025) at most 8 year-level regressors fit; the 11 series together are not identifiable. Hence two specifications: (i) **main**: 4 series, one per dimension (interest, inflation, activity, employment); (ii) **full**: the 11 series summarised in 3 principal components (Jolliffe, 2002). The model with year dummies is the reference; the macro models are nested in it, and the likelihood-ratio test says whether the macro series reproduce all the variation across years.

**Inference.** Robust standard errors clustered by CDA (Cameron & Miller, 2015). Since the macro variation comes from only 9 years, the micro p-values of the macro series are optimistic (Moulton, 1990). Conservative column: **two-step** regression of the 9 year effects of the reference model on the macro series (OLS; Donald & Lang, 2007).

**Window.** Ends in 2025 (the lab window). Conditional association, not causal effect.

#### 8.7.4 How to read the aggregate series (PGE view) {#edac-how-to-read-the-aggregate-series-pge-view}

Three simple charts, **no dual axis**:

1. **Stock** (`fig_estoque_agregado_ano`): how much the VAT (ICMS) portfolio owes each year (BRL billion).
2. **Collections** (`fig_serie_agregada_icms`): how much came in through GARE in the year (BRL billion).
3. **Portfolio recovery rate** (`fig_painel_taxa_media_ano`, the same series as `fig_taxa_recuperacao_anual` / `extra_taxa_carteira`): Σ collected ÷ Σ stock in the year (~0.2%–0.7%/year typical).

The portfolio recovery rate is the metric for the conversation with PGE. The arithmetic mean of the per-CDA ratios (`taxa_media_id` in the CSV) explodes with residual stock and should **not** be used as portfolio recovery.

If the recovery rate falls while the stock rises, the debt "grows" faster than collection: a descriptive reading, no causality. The window ends in 2025.

### 8.8 Domain, GARE over the life of the debt and macro series {#edac-domain-gare-over-the-life-of-the-debt-and-macro-series}

Her request, in this order: (1) **correlation with macro series** (Selic, IPCA, unemployment, GDP and the rest of the basket); (2) stock **without counting the same CDA twice**; (3) domain questions (age, type of payment timing, enrolment calendar).

**Fast path — run from 7A to the synthesis.** `painel_icms_completo.parquet` is already one row per `ID_DEBITO` × `ano`. Stock, age and sanity checks come from it (Polars). The monthly Y for the macro series is `VALOR_RECEITA` from `ARRECADACAO` restricted to the IDs of this panel, not a month-by-month stock in `DEBITO`.

Honest time for this run: **about 45–75 min**. The bulk is the collections semi-join (7C) and the GARE join with the enrolment date (7C2). The one-month probe on `DEBITO` (the cell after 7A) can take ~15–40 min if the year/month filter does not prune the scan; it can be switched off with `RODAR_PROBE_RAW = False`.

**Do not switch on** `RODAR_7A_SLOW` / `RODAR_7C_SLOW` at the end if the deadline is ~1 hour. These cells scan `DEBITO` month by month (hours, a well-resourced machine / Pontal). They start switched off: Run all does not trigger the scan. They are not part of the DoD.

DuckDB, when it appears: `temp_directory` in `DATA_ROOT/_duckdb_tmp_eda`, `max_temp_directory_size=80GiB`, `memory_limit=1500MB`, `threads=1`, `preserve_insertion_order=false`. An artefact already written is skipped.

If this Jupyter tab was opened before the edit, reload the file from disk and do not save the old version over it.

#### 8.8.1 Stock sanity check (fast, annual panel grain) {#edac-a-stock-sanity-check-fast-annual-panel-grain}

`DEBITO` repeats the CDA in every extraction. The panel **already** has 1 row per `ID_DEBITO` × `ano` (mean value in that year). Here we only check, by `ano`: `n_rows`, `n_unique(ID_DEBITO)` and the sum of `estoque_medio`. Expected: `n_rows` ≈ `n_unique`.

There is no month-by-month scan. This is on purpose: the stock sanity check used in the analyses is the one at this annual grain.

#### 8.8.3 How to read the sanity check {#edac-how-to-read-the-sanity-check}

In the panel, `linhas_por_id` ≈ 1 in each year: summing `estoque` does **not** count the same CDA twice in that year. A CDA can appear in several years (that is another question: age and permanence, not double-counting within the year).

The one-month probe, if it ran, is the raw table. `linhas_por_id_raw` ≫ 1 means repeated extraction. Do not use `n_linhas` from `DEBITO` as the number of debts.

#### 8.8.4 Domain in the VAT (ICMS) panel (fast) {#edac-b-domain-in-the-vat-icms-panel-fast}

The panel is VAT (ICMS) only (the VAT (ICMS) | IPVA | fees mapping stays in steps 2–3; here there is no type column and `DEBITO` is not scanned).

Cut-off = **last `ano` of the panel**, already 1 row per CDA. Age = 31/12 of that year − `data_inscricao`. `pago_no_ano`: `arrecadado` > 0 in that year. `ja_arrecadou`: some year of the panel with `arrecadado` > 0 (not the full history before the panel). The main domain chart is the **delay to the first GARE**: first observed year with collections minus the enrolment year. Seasonality = month of `data_inscricao`, once per CDA.

Do not interpret enrolment × GARE in the same year as data quality: payment often happens in later years.

#### 8.8.5 How to read age, open/paid, delay and Pareto {#edac-how-to-read-age-openpaid-delay-and-pareto}

Compare `n_id` with `estoque`. A `5a+` band that is large in value and small in GARE in the current year is an old portfolio, not proof that "it is not recovered early"; the GARE value window is in 7C2.

#### 8.8.6 First GARE (age at first payment) {#edac-first-gare-age-at-first-payment}

The chart of age at first GARE uses **only CDAs with at least one year of `arrecadado > 0`** and a non-negative delay. The percentage is within that group, not within all CDAs. CDAs with no observed GARE are left out of the curve: they do not count as "paid in year 0". The subtitle separates three populations: all CDAs in the panel, those with ≥1 GARE, and those with no observed GARE. This is not the subset still open in the cut-off year's stock.

The grain is **annual** (year of the first `arrecadado > 0` minus the year of `data_inscricao`). It is not the date of the GARE document; that date enters in 7C2. Payment before the first year of the panel is not seen.

#### 8.8.7 Settlement (proxy — there is no registration status) {#edac-settlement-proxy-there-is-no-registration-status}

The panel has no `situacao`, write-off date or settlement flag. These fields were not imputed.

**Proxy used:** the first year in which the CDA's sum of `arrecadado`, accumulated from the first year it appears in the panel, reaches the `estoque_medio` of that opening year (`estoque_abertura > 0`). The age is the year of that crossing minus the enrolment year.

The chart shows **only the CDAs for which the proxy fires**. CDAs with a valid opening stock that do not cross by the last observed year stay as **still open under the proxy**, outside the curve. A null or ≤ 0 opening stock leaves the proxy undefined (also outside). It is not an administrative write-off: the opening stock is not the value at the enrolment date when the CDA existed before the panel; later interest can raise the stock above what the proxy treats as covered; a stock reduction without corresponding collections does not fire the proxy.

#### 8.8.8 Enrolment cohort × years after enrolment {#edac-enrolment-cohort-years-after-enrolment}

The **lines by cohort** chart (enrolment year) replaces the heatmap. Each line is the cumulative percentage of the cohort with **some** GARE up to that number of years after enrolment. The denominator is **all CDAs of the cohort in the panel**, not only those that paid and not only those still open. Cohorts before the first year of the panel are left out, so as not to count as delay a GARE that the database does not see. Horizons not yet observable **do not enter the line** (they are not zero). Guides at 1, 3 and 5 years help the comparison across cohorts. PNG: `extra_coorte_horizonte.png` (regenerable from the CSV `dominio_coorte_horizonte_gare.csv` only).

`ja_arrecadou` looks at the years in the panel. Pareto: if a few per cent of IDs carry most of the stock, the mean does not describe the typical CDA.

Seasonality is the enrolment calendar (month), counting each CDA once. It is not the extraction flow.

#### 8.8.9 Flows: new CDAs, annual stock, monthly Y of collections {#edac-c-flows-new-cdas-annual-stock-monthly-y-of-collections}

The **monthly** stock in `DEBITO` is left out (7C-slow cell, switched off). The stock of this step = annual sum of the panel.

Monthly Y for the macro series = `n_pagadores` and `VALOR_RECEITA` in `ARRECADACAO`, panel IDs only (`SEMI JOIN`), spilling to Meedi.

`n_novas` on the fast path is the month of `data_inscricao` **already recorded in the panel** (once per CDA). Recounting this in `DEBITO` is a full table scan: `SKIP_NOVAS_DEBITO` starts as `True`. The annual proxy (first `ano` in which the id appears in the panel) goes to `novas_proxy_anual_painel.parquet` anyway. Lags 1–3 are of the monthly series, in calendar months (a gap becomes a zero flow).

**GARE coverage:** monthly collections have flows only from **2016-01**. The 2010–2015 spine fills months with `arrec_receita=0` / `n_pagadores=0` because of early enrolment; it is **not** "zero collected, observed". Charts and the macro×Y join (7E) cut at `mes >= 2016-01`. The full parquet may still keep the long spine for inspection.

#### 8.8.10 7C2 — In which window of the debt's life does the GARE occur? {#edac-c2-in-which-window-of-the-debts-life-does-the-gare-occur}

**Sample, stated on the chart:** GARE from `ARRECADACAO` with a valid date, restricted to the VAT (ICMS) CDAs that are in the panel and have `data_inscricao`. All these payments enter. It is **not** a subset of open CDAs, **nor** of those that paid only in the cut-off year, **nor** of "paid only". CDAs that never had a GARE contribute no value, but enter the denominator of the share by window if their observed age reaches the start of the window.

Age at payment = GARE date − the **panel's** `data_inscricao` (map of `ID_DEBITO`, earliest date), not a `GROUP BY` on `DEBITO`. Windows: 0–3m, 3–12m, 1–3y, 3–5y, 5+.

`pct_valor` splits `VALOR_RECEITA` **among the GAREs of this join**. The denominator is the sum of these payments, not the stock.

The second figure is a share of CDAs: IDs with at least one GARE in the window, divided by the IDs whose age up to the last year of the panel reaches the **start** of the window (open or not). It is not Kaplan–Meier and **not a recovery rate** (`arrecadado / estoque`). Old debt, enrolled before the panel's coverage, enters the denominator of the short windows even though we have not seen the start of its life, so the 0–3m share is underestimated. Read it together with `pct_valor`, which does not depend on this denominator.

#### 8.8.11 How to read the GARE windows {#edac-how-to-read-the-gare-windows}

Both charts use the same join: **VAT (ICMS) panel × GARE** (`ARRECADACAO`), CDAs with an enrolment date. The sample is not restricted to open CDAs, nor to those that paid in the cut-off year. CDAs that never had a GARE are outside `pct_valor` (there is no value to split) and inside the denominator of the share, if their observed age reaches the window.

`pct_valor` says where the collected money is in this join: early (0–12 months) or in old debt (5y+). This is not a causal effect of collection policy.

The second bar is a **share of CDAs with GARE**, not a recovery rate. It is discrete by window, with the short-window bias mentioned above (debt enrolled before the coverage enters the denominator without the start of its life observed). If `pct_valor` and this share tell different stories, describe both; do not pick the one that fits better.

#### 8.8.12 CDA age × recovery / stock {#edac-d-cda-age-recovery-stock}

Age at 31/12 of the row's year. Pearson/Spearman correlations at the micro level; the chart uses the **portfolio recovery rate by band** (Σcollected/Σstock). The median of the per-CDA ratios is ~0 and is not plotted.

#### 8.8.13 Macro series {#edac-e-macro-series}

`MACRO` in `macro.duckdb`, monthly mean (Selic and PTAX are daily). Codes: Selic 432, IPCA 433, IGP-M 189, GDP 4380, unemployment 24369, employed 24379, PTAX 1, corporate credit 20540, household debt 29037, debt service 29034, IPCA-15 7478.

Monthly join with the 7C Y (`arrec_receita`, `n_pagadores`, `n_novas`). For each pair: level, monthly difference, and Y lagged 1, 2 and 3 months. The annual check uses the annual mean and the December value of the macro variable against the panel aggregates (one row per CDA×year: the summed stock does not duplicate IDs within the year).

Micro panel of the **recovery rate by CDA × year** (zeros = no GARE) and all/payers/portfolio × macro correlations: see **7F**.

The four monthly heatmaps read a different lag: for each k = 0, 1, 2 and 3, Pearson between the flow in month t (`arrec_receita`, `n_pagadores`, `n_novas`, if they exist) and the macro in t−k. The macro leads Y. The monthly series **has no mean recovery rate**; that Y is only in the annual block of 7F, in four other heatmaps, with the same convention, from `taxa_recuperacao_anual_agg`.

**Window:** the monthly macro×Y join uses `mes >= 2016-01` (GARE covered; avoids the zeros of the 2010–15 spine).

#### 8.8.14 How to read macro × debt {#edac-how-to-read-macro-debt}

Correlation is not effect. Series in levels mix common trends (prices, portfolio scale, nominal GDP). What matters for the conversation is whether the sign **survives in Δ** and whether the lagged Y (collections themselves, lagged) does not absorb the association.

A possible reading, still descriptive: higher Selic or unemployment together with lower collections is consistent with expensive credit and a weaker ability to pay; it does not identify the Selic as a cause. IPCA or IGP-M together with a larger stock may be monetary correction of the claim, not "more evasion". PTAX and corporate credit enter as context of cost and of the firm's financial slack, not as a lever.

Monthly and annual results need not agree. Different frequency, different composition. If they disagree, record the disagreement.

In the monthly heatmap, k is the lag of the **macro**: Y in month t against the macro in t−k. k = 0 is contemporaneous. A signal that appears at k > 0 and weakens at k = 0 is consistent with the macro leading the flow; it is still association. The long table of this passage still has the lagged Y and the monthly difference; that convention is not the heatmaps'. The mean recovery rate does not enter here because the monthly series does not have it.

#### 8.8.15 Recovery rate panel by CDA × year {#edac-f-recovery-rate-panel-by-cda-year}

`painel_icms_completo.parquet` is the micro recovery panel: one row per `ID_DEBITO` × `ano`, with `taxa = arrecadado / estoque_medio`. No GARE in that year → `arrecadado = 0` → **`taxa = 0`** (the CDA does not disappear from the base).

**Main reading for the portfolio:** use the **portfolio recovery rate** = Σ collected / Σ estoque_medio. It weights each CDA by its stock and answers "how much of the portfolio was recovered?". In the stakeholder chart (`fig_painel_taxa_media_ano`), this is the **only** series, with an automatic axis.

The arithmetic mean of `taxa` is not portfolio recovery. About 0.5% of rows have a tiny residual stock (approx. BRL 1–4) and a high GARE, producing ratios of `10^4–10^5`; a few outliers push the simple mean above 100%. In other words, **arithmetic mean of ratios ≠ portfolio recovery**. In this base, Σ collected / Σ stock is roughly 0.2–0.7% and is the appropriate measure for the conversation with stakeholders.

The metrics `taxa_media_all` and `taxa_media_pagadores` stay in the aggregate/CSV for diagnostics only; they do **not** enter the chart for PGE.

Unit of analysis = **CDA × year** (not month × CDA). The monthly Y of 7E is still the portfolio (`n_pagadores`, `arrec_receita`). Here we save a slim parquet for Stata/later and correlate aggregate annual series × macro series, including the portfolio recovery rate in the previous year and earlier years.

#### 8.8.16 How to read the recovery rate (CDA × year panel) {#edac-how-to-read-the-recovery-rate-cda-year-panel}

- **`taxa = 0`**: there was no GARE in that year for the CDA.
- **Portfolio recovery rate** = Σ collected / Σ stock in the year: it is the number in the chart (~tenths of a %).
- The mean of the per-CDA ratios can exceed 100% with tiny residual stock; do **not** use it as recovery.
- Median of the per-CDA ratios ≈ 0 (most without payment): only in the diagnostic print, outside the stakeholder chart.

#### 8.8.17 Synthesis (fill in after running — fast path) {#edac-synthesis-fill-in-after-running-fast-path}

Descriptive text. No management recommendation and no causality.

1. Sanity: `linhas_por_id` in the panel = ?. If ≈ 1, the annual stock does not duplicate IDs within the year. One-month probe on `DEBITO`, if any: `linhas_por_id_raw` = ? (repeated extraction; does not enter the sum).
2. VAT (ICMS) stock in the last year of the panel and Pareto (share of CDAs for 50/80/90% of the value) = ?.
3. Open vs with GARE in that year (`arrecadado` > 0), and what changes when the criterion is "has collected in some year of the panel".
4. Window that concentrates the GARE `pct_valor` = ?. `hazard_id` in the short windows = ?; remember the exposure bias of old debts.
5. Age × rate: Pearson = ?, Spearman (sample) = ?.
6. Macro series: largest monthly |Pearson| in levels and which survive in Δ and with Y lag 1–3 = ?. Do the annual mean and December agree with the monthly? Where they disagree, keep both readings.
7. **Recovery rate (7F):** CDA×year panel = `painel_taxa_recuperacao_cda_ano.parquet` (zeros = no GARE). `taxa_carteira` in the last year = ?; median and means of the per-CDA ratios stay as diagnostics (sensitive to residual stock). Largest annual |Pearson| portfolio/median × macro (and whether the Y lag absorbs the signal) = ?.

New models are outside this step.

#### 8.8.18 DoD — step 7 (fast path) {#edac-dod-step-7-fast-path}

Required in this run (target ~1 h, without scanning `DEBITO` month by month):

- [ ] 7A: `sanidade_painel_anual.parquet` with `n_rows` ≈ `n_unique` per year
- [ ] 7A-probe: `sanidade_probe_raw_um_mes.parquet` **or** the cell skipped on purpose (`RODAR_PROBE_RAW=False` / interrupted); it does not block the rest
- [ ] 7B: `dominio_faixa_etaria.csv`, `dominio_aberto_pago.csv`, `dominio_inscricao_aberto_pago.csv`, `pareto_icms.csv`, `sazonalidade_inscricao_icms.csv`
- [ ] 7C: `estoque_anual_painel.parquet`, `serie_mensal_icms.parquet` (Y = collections, lags 1–3), `novas_proxy_anual_painel.parquet`. Scan of new CDAs in `DEBITO` only if `SKIP_NOVAS_DEBITO=False`
- [ ] 7C2: `gare_janela_vida_icms.csv` (windows + `hazard_id`)
- [ ] 7D: `corr_idade_pearson.csv`, `corr_idade_spearman.csv`
- [ ] 7E: `corr_macro_mensal.csv`, `corr_macro_anual_painel.csv` (mean and December), synthesis filled in
- [ ] 7F: `painel_taxa_recuperacao_cda_ano.parquet` (slim CDA×year), `taxa_recuperacao_anual_agg.parquet`, `corr_taxa_recuperacao_macro_anual.csv` (all / payers / portfolio × macro series, Y lags 1–3)

Outside the DoD (flags start as `False`; Pontal / overnight):

- 7A-slow → `sanidade_estoque_mensal.parquet`
- 7C-slow → `estoque_mensal_debito_opcional.parquet`

### 8.9 7-slow — optional, off-hours {#edac-slow-optional-off-hours}

The cells below are **not** part of the DoD. `RODAR_7A_SLOW` and `RODAR_7C_SLOW` start as `False`: you can run the cell, it only warns and exits. The month-by-month scan of `DEBITO` is for a well-resourced machine (Pontal), with `threads=1`, `memory_limit=1500MB`, temporaries on Meedi, parts and skip-if-exists.

Do not switch both on the same night without need: both re-read `DEBITO` by year-month. 7A-slow already brings the count and the deduplicated stock; 7C-slow only rewrites the stock series in another parquet.

#### 8.9.1 monthly stock in DEBITO (run later on Pontal) {#edac-a-slow-monthly-stock-in-debito-run-later-on-pontal}

Same sanity check as the old version: for each extraction year-month, `n_linhas` vs `n_id` and the stock after 1 row per `ID_DEBITO`. Parts in `eda_completo_artifacts/_sanidade_parts/`. Do not run it if the fast path is still missing.

::: {#edac-5b11f81f .cell execution_count=44}

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}
```
DO NOT RUN NOW if you need the rest of step 7 in about 1 hour. This scans DEBITO month by month (threads=1, memory_limit=1500MB, max_temp=80GiB, parts with skip-if-exists). Leave it for Pontal. With RODAR_7A_SLOW=False the cell does not query DEBITO.
skip 7A-slow.
```

:::


#### 8.9.2 monthly stock in DEBITO (run later on Pontal) {#edac-c-slow-monthly-stock-in-debito-run-later-on-pontal}

Series `n_estoque` / `estoque` by extraction month, VAT (ICMS), 1 row per `ID_DEBITO` within the month. Writes `estoque_mensal_debito_opcional.parquet` and does **not** touch `serie_mensal_icms.parquet` (that is the fast Y of collections). Parts in `_estoque_mensal_parts/`.
